body_markdown:
Engines are both surprisingly durable and shockingly fragile, and much of the swing between the two ends of that spectrum can be attributed to the oil inside any given engine being able to do its job by keeping friction, heat, and debris at bay. That means using good oil but also keeping that oil clean. It’s been over a century since engineers figured out that oil is best filtered, but do we as drivers and shade-tree mechanics actually grasp what’s going on inside[an oil filter](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/the-best-tools-to-remove-stuck-on-oil-filters/comment-page-4/) ?


Understanding oil is complex, and wrapping one’s head around filtration can be even tougher once you get past the “filter removes debris” level of comprehension. Luckily, we don’t have to become experts just to keep our daily driver running and instead can listen to experts like Lake Speed Jr., who goes by “The Motor Oil Geek” on YouTube. His latest video dives into filtration and involves a deep conversation with an engineer from Donaldson filtration about how filters work and why the media inside the can is critical to engine longevity.


The basis is around how that media is actually filtering. Oil filters work by sieving, or passing the oil through a medium that has holes small enough for the oil particles to pass through but the debris suspended in the oil will be caught and held. That[material ranges greatly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/toilet-paper-in-an-oil-filter-is-actually-a-good-idea/) , but one of the most popular options is cellulose fiber—what you might commonly call paper. Of course, like all the other parts of an automobile that have been around for a century, there is a lot more to it than folding up a sheet of paper, stuffing it into a can, and pushing oil through.


The filter media from inside a used oil filter.


[Phillip Thomas](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/pthomas/)


This media traps debris as oil flows through.


[Phillip Thomas](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/pthomas/)


Keeping quality oil filters on your car is important.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


That’s where the lab at Donaldson comes in. The Motor Oil Geek takes a trip through the lab and gets to see how the filtering media is actually made and tested. A relatively simple test bench does the heavy lifting, or more accurately, pumping, of hydraulic oil that is kept at 104 degrees Fahrenheit to replicate roughly 40-weight oil in an engine at operating temperature. The testing is broken into two parts, but the key bit we all think about is efficiency. The efficiency of a filter is determined not just by whether it removes the debris from the oil, but how much of variously sized debris it catches. No filter is perfect, but different engines and usage conditions might call for different filters due to the particle size of the debris expected to end up in the oil.


Oil filters are simple, yet quite complex. Is it just some paper in a can that oil flows through? Yes, but also no. That paper is actually finely tuned to get out the all the junk that needs to leave, without causing other problems along the way. Keeping the oil flowing is critical to a long-lasting engine, and that means the material inside your filter might be even more important than oil itself.
